title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve middle school mathematics learning, especially for students from low-income backgrounds, and whether the benefits differ by prior achievement. The authors frame the problem as a persistent equity and access challenge: tutoring is effective but expensive and difficult to scale, while AI-based math software alone may not sufficiently engage students who need the most support.

To address this, the study evaluates a hybrid model in which students use adaptive math software while human tutors provide motivational, relational, and content support. The system is implemented in three separate urban U.S. middle school settings using different platforms: IXL, i-Ready, and Carnegie Learning’s MATHia. Across the sites, the tutoring format varied from round-robin human support to a dashboard-guided model, allowing comparison of software-only conditions versus software plus teacher support versus software plus teacher and tutor support. The sample includes 125 students in Pennsylvania, 385 students in California, and 75 students in a Pennsylvania charter school, with students largely from low-income backgrounds and with site-specific racial/ethnic compositions.

The authors report that hybrid human-AI tutoring generally increased engagement and learning-process indicators such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, and lesson completion. They also find evidence of subgroup effects: lower-pretest or below-grade-level students benefited more than higher-pretest students, while the presence of a math teacher during software use tended to benefit higher-pretest students more. The paper concludes that hybrid tutoring is promising for improving middle school math learning at relatively low cost, and that dashboard-guided systems and better allocation of tutor attention may further strengthen equity and effectiveness.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed three-study quasi-experimental investigation with repeated measures and mixed-effects models, but it lacks random assignment and includes site-specific implementation differences and small samples at some sites. The design is stronger than simple correlational work, but not RCT-level evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects on math engagement and lesson progression are practically meaningful and directly relevant to a priority middle school population from low-income backgrounds. Several reported effects are at or above a medium magnitude in the learning-process domain, particularly the increases in time on task and workspaces completed per hour.

interventions.use_case: hybrid human-AI tutoring in middle school math using adaptive practice software (IXL, i-Ready, MATHia) paired with remote human tutor support and, in one site, a live tutor dashboard

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental middle school sites, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software only. In Site 1 (n=125), mixed-effects models found tutoring increased time spent practicing (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]) and improved skills proficient, with stronger benefits for lower pretest students (pretest:Tutoring β=-0.212, 95% CI [-0.325, -0.096]). In Site 2 (n=385), tutoring increased weekly minutes on task from 24 to 33 and increased lessons passed, especially for below-grade-level students (lesson_grade:during_treatment β=-0.05261, p=0.000217). In Site 3 (n=75), moving from 1:8 to 1:4 tutor:student ratio increased MATHia workspaces completed per hour by 0.36 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: IXL time spent, questions answered, skills proficient; i-Ready time on task and lessons passed; MATHia workspaces completed per hour
finding.study_size: n=585 total across three sites (Site 1 n=125, Site 2 n=385, Site 3 n=75)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports consistent gains in engagement and participation, which it treats as a core mechanism linking tutoring to learning. In Site 1, tutoring significantly increased time spent on software, and in Site 2 weekly time on task rose from 24 to 33 minutes during treatment, suggesting higher engagement with the math platform. The authors interpret these changes as increased learning opportunities and improved participation, especially for lower-performing students.
finding.measure: time spent on task, engagement/participation with math software
finding.study_size: n=585 total across three sites (Site 1 n=125, Site 2 n=385, Site 3 n=75)
finding.effect_size: β=0.202 for time spent; 24 to 33 minutes/week

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the hybrid model can increase the efficiency of tutoring delivery by enabling more student progress with a lower tutor:student ratio and using dashboard-guided support. In Site 3, reducing the tutor:student ratio from about 1:8 to 1:4 increased progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]), indicating better throughput when tutors had more availability. The authors also frame the model as scalable and lower-cost than exclusive human tutoring, with estimated marginal costs around $700 per student annually.
finding.measure: workspaces completed per hour; tutor:student ratio; estimated marginal cost per student
finding.study_size: n=75 for Site 3; cost estimate across three sites
